statement: Ana cuts a 2 cm square off one corner of a paper square with 6 cm sides. What is the distance all the way round the shape that is left?

choices.misconception: I took away the 2 cm and 2 cm cut off the outside edges, but forgot the two new 2 cm edges inside the corner.
I added the two new 2 cm edges but did not take away the 2 cm and 2 cm cut off the outside edges.
I added all four sides of the small square to the 24 cm of the big square.
I worked out 6 times 6, which counts the small squares inside, not the distance round.

hints: Walk all the way round the new shape and write down each side.
Draw the shape after the corner is gone. Cutting the corner takes away two bits of the old edge but makes two new edges. Compare what is lost with what is gained.
Put the cut corner at the top right and start at the bottom left. Go 6 cm along the bottom, 4 cm up, 2 cm in, 2 cm up, 4 cm along the top and 6 cm down. Add these sides.

solutions.reliable: Put the cut corner at the top right. Going round from the bottom left corner, the sides are 6 cm along the bottom, 4 cm up, 2 cm in, 2 cm up, 4 cm along the top and 6 cm down. That is $6 + 4 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 6 = 24$ cm, the same as the whole square. The idea to keep: list every side of the new shape, including the new edges made by the cut.
solutions.elegant: The new edge going across is as long as the 2 cm missing from the top, and the new edge going up is as long as the 2 cm missing from the side. So nothing is lost and nothing is gained: the distance round is still $6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24$ cm. The idea to keep: cutting a square out of a corner makes the shape smaller but keeps the distance round the same.

whyOnTest: Cutting a corner out of a square leaves the distance round unchanged, which surprises students who expect a smaller shape to have a shorter border.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
